books.section: Topic 7.4 The Progressives — The Progressive Response to the Triangle Factory Fire
The Progressive Era and World War I (1900-1920)

stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 9, and 5 Steps to a 5 2024, Chapter 20.
stimulus.text: Paraphrase of Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 9, and 5 Steps to a 5 2024, Chapter 20: On March 25, 1911, fire swept through the Triangle Shirtwaist Factory on the upper floors of a building in New York City. Most of the workers were young women, many of them recent Italian or Jewish immigrants. One exit was blocked by flames and another was locked, and a fire escape collapsed. In the end, 146 workers died. The tragedy led New York to pass fire safety laws and to the rapid growth of the garment workers' union.

rationales.A: The fire was in a New York garment factory. Coal miners worked underground in Pennsylvania, not in shirtwaist shops.
rationales.B: The passage says most of the workers were young women, many of them recent Italian or Jewish immigrants, making shirtwaists in a New York factory.
rationales.C: Railroad engineers worked on trains and tracks. The Triangle workers sewed garments on the upper floors of a city building.
rationales.D: Farm laborers worked Southern fields. The Triangle workers were city garment workers, mostly young immigrant women.
rationales.general:
1. Read the passage's own description. The workers were young women, many of them recent Italian or Jewish immigrants.
2. Match the workplace. They made shirtwaists in a New York garment factory.
3. Rule out the other workplaces. Mines, railroads, and farms had their own dangers and their own workers.
Remember: a passage that describes its people directly is giving you the answer, so take the description as stated.
